text.p: Afghanistan's hardline Islamic Taleban militia said on Tuesday it had told former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood to surrender or be wiped out of his valley stronghold north of Kabul.
Commander Abdur Razzaq told Reuters at his headquarters at the mouth of the Panjsher valley he had sent a letter to Masood saying that if he stopped fighting "we will forgive him".

"(But) if he goes on fighting, we will clear the area of his presence," said Razzaq, commander of Taleban's forces which have swept 75 km (50 miles) north of Kabul in the past few days and bottled up Masood in the Panjsher valley.
The Taleban now control more than three-quarters of war-weary Afghanistan after capturing the capital on Friday with barely a shot fired.
They have named a six-man interim "shura" or council to run Afghanistan as a strict Islamic state.
Razzaq said no time limit had been set for Masood to reply, but that he was busy planning an assault on the valley which Masood defended successfully against Soviet forces in the 1980s.

Razzaq declined to say when the assault might begin, but Taleban fighters said they had already received orders to move early on Wednesday in two directions -- against the Panjsher and against Uzbek forces of General Abdul Rashid Dostum further north up the Salang highway.
"The orders have been given. We move against the Panjsher and Dostum early tomorrow. Everything is ready," said one Taleban fighter.
Razzaq said he did not want to fight the Uzbek forces of Dostum, whose headquarters are in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, however.

As the Taleban pushed north along the Salang highway from Jabal os-Siraj, a small green oasis in a khaki landscape of rugged, treeless mountains, Dostum sent forces on Monday south of the Salang tunnel, a key choke point on the road from Kabul to central Asia.
Taleban fighters said another ultimatum had been sent to the Uzbeks to withdraw to their previous positions by 4 p.m. (1130 GMT) on Tuesday or be attacked.
But Razzaq said it had been sent without the authorisation of the Taleban high command and was not valid.
Uzbek commander Atiqullah told Reuters at the Salang tunnel there was no question of allowing the Taleban to move through.

"Civilians are welcome to pass through, but if the Taleban come with force we will fight them," he said in the narrow, rocky Salang path through the Hindu Kush, where the wind is already edged with a winter chill.
Atiqullah was scornful of the Taleban's brand of Islam, which contrasts sharply with the more relaxed attitude of the Uzbeks.
"All these things they are doing, like telling women they can't work and demanding men grow beards, do you think this is appropriate for the 20th century?" asked the beardless Uzbek.
If the Taleban do resume their assault, they could be in for some of the hardest fighting since their movement was born in religious schools in Pakistan refugee camps two years ago.
Dostum and Masood have the only major forces still ranged against the Taleban and are the two generals with the most formidable reputation.

The Soviet forces backing a then-communist government could never wrest control of the Panjsher from Masood, who is now preparing to defend it against the Taleban, Reuter TV correspondent Laurent Hamida reported from inside the valley.

He said Masood's men had blown in the side of the narrow gorge leading on to the valley to form a rock barrier across the road and were busy blowing up more sections of it inside the valley on Tuesday.
But he said the local population expected heavy fighting and hundreds were packing up and trying to leave the valley.
It was not clear whether Masood still had the men with the morale and equipment for a lengthy defence after his headlong flight from Kabul since Friday.
Razzaq said he had no information on Masood's strength and would not disclose his own.
